clinicalPearls: Presents as striking concentric, whorled erythematous bands with a fine trailing scale, producing a 'wood-grain' or 'zebra-stripe' pattern
The eruption migrates rapidly, sometimes several centimetres per day, and is usually widespread and pruritic
It is one of the most specific paraneoplastic dermatoses and should prompt an urgent search for internal malignancy
Lung carcinoma is the most frequently associated tumour, followed by oesophageal, breast and other cancers
The rash often precedes the diagnosis of the underlying cancer, so recognition offers a chance for earlier detection
Biopsy shows non-specific changes such as a perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate with spongiosis and parakeratosis, so diagnosis is largely clinical
Treatment of the underlying tumour typically clears the eruption, whereas symptomatic measures alone are of limited benefit
reference.pathophysiology: Erythema gyratum repens is considered a paraneoplastic phenomenon in which tumour-associated antigens are thought to trigger an immune response that cross-reacts with skin antigens, producing a migrating figurate erythema. Immune complex deposition and altered cutaneous antigen expression have been proposed as mechanisms. The rapidly shifting concentric wave-like erythema reflects a dynamic hypersensitivity reaction in the skin, and the close temporal link with an underlying, often occult, malignancy is central to its behaviour.
additionalInvestigations: Urgent search for internal malignancy including chest imaging
Age- and risk-appropriate cancer screening (breast, gastrointestinal, gynaecological)
Skin biopsy to exclude specific mimics
Direct immunofluorescence to exclude bullous pemphigoid
Full blood count, inflammatory markers and general health screen
redFlags: The eruption itself, given its very high association with underlying cancer
Weight loss, cough, haemoptysis or other symptoms of internal malignancy
Failure of the rash to respond, implying an undetected or untreated tumour
reference.prognosis: The skin prognosis is favourable once the underlying malignancy is treated, with the eruption usually resolving; however, overall prognosis is dominated by the frequently advanced associated cancer, so the outlook depends chiefly on tumour stage and treatability.
pitfalls: Treating the rash symptomatically without pursuing the mandatory malignancy workup
Confusing it with the slower, less florid erythema annulare centrifugum
Stopping the cancer search after an initial negative screen when the rash persists
Overlooking a paraneoplastic cause because biopsy findings are non-specific
